title: Mantou
subtitle: Plain Chinese steamed buns with a pillowy, slightly sweet crumb
excerpt: Mantou steams in 15 minutes and has no crust. The dough is slightly enriched with sugar and requires thorough kneading so the gluten can hold the shape during steaming. The buns go into the steamer cold rather than hot, rising slowly as the water comes to a boil.
sourceNotes: Mantou are plain steamed wheat buns fundamental to northern Chinese cooking, distinct from filled baozi. They are served as a starch alongside savoury dishes or eaten at breakfast with congee. The technique of starting buns in a cold steamer is the standard published method and avoids the collapse caused by a sudden blast of steam.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze cooled buns in a bag. Steam from frozen for 8 to 10 minutes, or microwave for 60 to 90 seconds wrapped in a damp paper towel.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles cleanly. Use two steamer tiers if available; do not crowd the buns as they will stick together as they expand.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Shaped, unsteamed buns can be covered and kept in the fridge for up to 12 hours. Steam directly from the fridge, adding 2 minutes to the cooking time.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Steamed over boiling water. Start buns in a cold steamer, bring to a boil, then steam over vigorous steam for 15 minutes.

glossaryTerms.definition: The second rise for steamed buns (mantou, baozi) is shorter than for baked bread. Twenty to thirty minutes is enough; the dough should grow by 50 per cent, not double. Over-proofing causes the buns to collapse when they hit the steam.

content.text: Mantou requires more kneading than most bread doughs. The gluten must be well-developed so the buns hold their shape during steaming rather than collapsing. The
is shorter than for a baked loaf; stop when the buns look noticeably puffed but have not doubled. Going too far makes them collapse.

Combine the flour, yeast, sugar, and salt. Add the warm water and mix until a dough forms. Knead for 10 minutes until the dough is very smooth, elastic, and slightly glossy. It should pass the windowpane test: stretch a small piece thin enough to see light through it without it tearing.
Cover and leave at room temperature for 30 minutes until slightly puffed.
Roll the dough into a log about 5 cm in diameter. Cut into 8 equal pieces. Shape each piece into a smooth oval bun, pulling the surface taut from the top and pinching the seam underneath.
Place each bun on a small square of baking paper in the steamer basket. Leave 4 cm between buns. Proof uncovered for 20 minutes.

Place the steamer basket over the pan. Add cold water to the pan. Put the lid on and turn the heat to medium-high. Bring the water to a boil with the buns inside; do not let the steam hit them before the water is fully boiling.

Once the water is boiling, steam for 15 minutes over vigorous heat without lifting the lid. Turn off the heat and wait 5 minutes before opening to avoid the buns collapsing from the sudden temperature change.

attrs.title: Do not open the lid mid-steam

content.text: Opening the lid while the buns are steaming causes a sudden drop in temperature and pressure. The buns will wrinkle and collapse on the surface. If you must check, wait until the full cooking time has elapsed.
